How fast is manifoldsR against what R users actually reach for? This article
collects the speed comparisons that used to sit at the end of each vignette.
It is not shipped with the package and only rendered for the website. The
competitor packages are listed under `Config/Needs/benchmarks` in DESCRIPTION,
and the UMAP and PHATE comparisons additionally need Python via `reticulate`.
Every chunk only runs if its packages are installed.

All timings are single runs on synthetic data from one machine, so take them
as orders of magnitude, not as precise numbers.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(manifoldsR)

has_bench <- requireNamespace("microbenchmark", quietly = TRUE)
has_py <- requireNamespace("reticulate", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: python env
#| eval: !expr has_bench && has_py
# set up the venv for the Python part/dependencies
local({
  env_name <- "r-manifolds"
  py_pkgs <- c("phate", "umap-learn", "numpy", "scipy")

  if (!reticulate::virtualenv_exists(env_name)) {
    reticulate::virtualenv_create(env_name)
    reticulate::virtualenv_install(env_name, packages = py_pkgs)
  }

  if (!reticulate::py_available()) {
    reticulate::use_virtualenv(env_name, required = TRUE)
  }

  missing_pkgs <- Filter(
    Negate(reticulate::py_module_available),
    c("phate", "umap")
  )
  if (length(missing_pkgs) > 0L) {
    reticulate::virtualenv_install(env_name, packages = py_pkgs)
  }
})
```

## Nearest neighbour searches

Let's just have a look on how the different kNN methods perform on different
sizes.

```{r}
#| label: knn - benchmark 1000
#| eval: !expr has_bench
k <- 10L

cluster_data <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "cluster",
  n_samples = 1000L
)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  exhaustive = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = cluster_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "exhaustive",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  kmknn = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = cluster_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "kmknn",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  annoy = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = cluster_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "annoy",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  hnsw = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = cluster_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "hnsw",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  balltree = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = cluster_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "balltree",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  nndescent = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = cluster_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "nndescent",
      nn_params = params_nn(extract_knn = TRUE),
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  ivf = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = cluster_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "ivf",
      nn_params = params_nn(),
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L # single comparison for speed
)
```

On small datasets, the exhaustive search beats everything. We need to build
the indices in the other methods, a cost that only makes sense when we have
sufficient samples to do this. Otherwise, modern CPUs with SIMD can do the
necessary `O(N^2)` in no time on smaller datasets. What about 50k cells?

```{r}
#| label: knn - benchmark 50k
#| eval: !expr has_bench
benchmark_data <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "cluster",
  n_samples = 50000L
)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  exhaustive = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "exhaustive",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  kmknn = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "kmknn",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  annoy = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "annoy",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  hnsw = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "hnsw",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  balltree = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "balltree",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  nndescent = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "nndescent",
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  ivf = {
    generate_knn_graph(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = k,
      knn_method = "ivf",
      nn_params = params_nn(n_probe = 25L),
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L # single comparison for speed
)
```

We start observing the first pattern, that the approximate nearest neighbour
searches are faster than the exhaustive search. The delta becomes more
pronounced with more samples:

## UMAP

How does the parallel Adam version compare against other UMAP
implementations? Let's do a benchmark:

```{r}
#| label: umap - benchmark small
#| eval: !expr has_bench && has_py && requireNamespace("umap", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("uwot", quietly = TRUE)
benchmark_data <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "cluster",
  n_samples = 5000L
)

umap_py <- reticulate::import("umap")

# initialise numba properly via JIT for fair comparison
# run a small dataset...
test_reducer <- umap_py$UMAP(
  n_neighbors = 15L,
  n_jobs = parallel::detectCores() - 1L
)
test <- test_reducer$fit_transform(benchmark_data$data[1:500, ])

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  # umap version in pure R
  umap = {
    umap::umap(
      d = benchmark_data$data,
      method = "naive"
    )
  },
  umap_reticulate = {
    reducer <- umap_py$UMAP(
      n_neighbors = 15L,
      n_jobs = parallel::detectCores() - 1L
    )
    reducer$fit_transform(benchmark_data$data)
  },
  # uwot - umap, for example used in Seurat
  uwot = {
    uwot::umap(X = benchmark_data$data)
  },
  # uwot - umap2 version with parallel Adam under the hood
  # the approach that was also taken by manifoldsR
  uwot_v2 = {
    uwot::umap2(X = benchmark_data$data)
  },
  # the manifolds version
  manifold_umap = {
    umap(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = 15L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L # single comparison for speed
)
```

We can appreciate that the standard R version is slow (as expected). If we
leverage the Python version (with numba behind the scenes) via reticulate,
we can get some speed ups (we need to however first JIT compile the numba
parts). However, the uwot v2 version and the manifold are the fastest here.
Let's pit them together against each other in a larger data set.

```{r}
#| label: umap - benchmark large
#| eval: !expr has_bench && requireNamespace("uwot", quietly = TRUE)
benchmark_data_2 <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "cluster",
  n_samples = 50000L
)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  # uwot - umap2, for example used in Seurat
  uwot_v2 = {
    uwot::umap2(X = benchmark_data_2$data)
  },
  manifold_umap = {
    umap(
      data = benchmark_data_2$data,
      k = 15L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L # single comparison for speed
)
```

Due to optimised memory layouts, aggressive in-lining, heavy parallelism and
look-up tables (LUTs), this version is **fast** and is likely(?) the fastest
UMAP available in R, while keeping memory usage minimal due to leveraging Rust
from the point that data is moved into the Rust kernel, until the embedding has
been fitted. No round tripping through R, just highly optimised and compiled
code throughout. The different nearest neighbour search algorithms give
additional flexibility.

## t-SNE

Let's compare the BH implementation in `manifoldsR` against `Rtsne` (the most
widely used t-SNE implementation in R, itself a wrapper around the C++ BH
t-SNE code). The `tsne` package (pure R, naive `O(N^2)` implementation) is
just too slow to be worth comparing here...

```{r}
#| label: tsne - benchmark small
#| eval: !expr has_bench && requireNamespace("Rtsne", quietly = TRUE)
benchmark_data <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "cluster",
  n_samples = 5000L
)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  Rtsne = {
    Rtsne::Rtsne(
      X = benchmark_data$data,
      dims = 2,
      perplexity = 30,
      verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  manifold_bh = {
    tsne(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      perplexity = 30,
      approx_type = "bh",
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  manifold_bh_qd = {
    tsne(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      perplexity = 30,
      approx_type = "bh_qd",
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L
)
```

The impact here is massive already. Let's see what happens with both BH and
both FFT versions? (To note, FFT's advantage becomes larger the bigger the data
set due to its near `O(N)` complexity.)

```{r}
#| label: tsne - benchmark large
#| eval: !expr has_bench
benchmark_data_large <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "cluster",
  n_samples = 75000L
)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  manifold_bh = {
    tsne(
      data = benchmark_data_large$data,
      perplexity = 30,
      approx_type = "bh",
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  manifold_bh_qd = {
    tsne(
      data = benchmark_data_large$data,
      perplexity = 30,
      approx_type = "bh_qd",
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  manifold_fft = {
    tsne(
      data = benchmark_data_large$data,
      perplexity = 30,
      approx_type = "fft",
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  manifold_fft_3k = {
    tsne(
      data = benchmark_data_large$data,
      perplexity = 30,
      approx_type = "fft_3k",
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L
)
```

The speed advantage of the Rust implementation comes from a combination of
optimised memory layout, aggressive inlining, and the fact that the entire
pipeline (kNN construction, probability computation and gradient descent)
runs within the Rust kernel without round-tripping through R. If you like
tSNE, but thought it's too slow... we got you.

## PHATE

Let's compare `manifoldsR` against `phateR` (the reference R implementation,
itself a wrapper around the Python `phate` library) on the trajectory data.

```{r}
#| label: phate - benchmark
#| eval: !expr has_bench && has_py && requireNamespace("phateR", quietly = TRUE)
benchmark_data <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "trajectory",
  n_samples = 10000L
)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  phateR = {
    phateR::phate(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      knn = 5L,
      n.jobs = -1,
      verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  manifold_phate = {
    phate(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = 5L,
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L
)
```

And on a larger data set with additionally the random landmark version

```{r}
#| label: phate - benchmark landmarks
#| eval: !expr has_bench && has_py && requireNamespace("phateR", quietly = TRUE)
benchmark_data_large <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "trajectory",
  n_samples = 100000L
)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  phateR = {
    phateR::phate(
      data = benchmark_data_large$data,
      knn = 5L,
      npca = 100L,
      n.jobs = -1,
      verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  manifold_phate_spectral = {
    phate(
      data = benchmark_data_large$data,
      k = 5L,
      knn_method = "nndescent", # good allrounder for larger data sets
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  manifold_phate_random = {
    phate(
      data = benchmark_data_large$data,
      k = 5L,
      knn_method = "nndescent", # good allrounder for larger data sets
      phate_params = params_phate(landmark_method = "random"),
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L
)
```

As with t-SNE and UMAP, the speed advantage of the Rust implementation comes
from the entire pipeline (kNN construction, kernel computation, diffusion and
MDS) running within the Rust kernel without round-tripping through Python in
this case. Usually, the differences become more pronounced with larger data
sets.

## PaCMAP

```{r}
#| label: pacmap - benchmark
#| eval: !expr has_bench
benchmark_data <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "cluster",
  n_samples = 10000L
)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  manifold_umap = {
    umap(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      k = 15L,
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  manifold_pacmap = {
    pacmap(
      data = benchmark_data$data,
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 3L
)
```

PaCMAP is generally slower than UMAP on the same data since it processes all
pairs every epoch rather than sampling. The three-phase schedule with 450
epochs (vs UMAP's 200 to 500) compounds this. For most datasets up to ~50k
samples this is not a concern in practice, but on very large data the
difference becomes noticeable.

## Diffusion maps

The most widely used R implementation of diffusion maps is
[`destiny`](https://bioconductor.org/packages/destiny/) (Bioconductor), which
implements the Haghverdi et al. variant aimed at single-cell data. However,
the installation of [`smoother`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=smoother),
a needed dependency of the package is not behaving at the moment. Hence, a
comparison could not be made here. We can still compare two different landmark
methods here on a larger data set.

```{r}
#| label: dm - benchmark landmarks
#| eval: !expr has_bench
benchmark_data_large <- manifold_synthetic_data(
  type = "trajectory",
  n_samples = 50000L
)

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  manifold_dm_spectral = {
    diffusion_maps(
      data = benchmark_data_large$data,
      k = 15L,
      knn_method = "nndescent",
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  manifold_dm_random = {
    diffusion_maps(
      data = benchmark_data_large$data,
      k = 15L,
      knn_method = "nndescent",
      dm_params = params_diffusion_maps(landmark_method = "random"),
      seed = 42L,
      .verbose = FALSE
    )
  },
  times = 1L
)
```

As elsewhere in `manifoldsR`, the speed gains come from keeping the whole
pipeline (kNN, kernel, diffusion, eigendecomposition, Nystroem extension)
inside the Rust kernel without bouncing through interpreted code. The gap
widens on larger data and becomes particularly pronounced once landmarks are
enabled.
